note: Step into the View and the uki-e box. Planes cut by hand by scripts/prep-views.py (a reconstruction); boxes are px in the 2048 px plane images; z in sheet heights (sheet = 2 units tall), 0 = the picture plane, negative = behind it.
what: Hiroshige built depth out of flat layers, not from one vanishing point. A large object cut by the sheet's edge sits in front (repoussoir); horizontal bands stack the middle distance; the viewpoint is often high, so the far ground climbs the sheet. Cutting a sheet into planes and moving your eye makes the stack visible. The cut is ours: the print was made flat, from woodblocks, and these planes are a reconstruction.

hv-099.title: Kinryūzan Temple at Asakusa
hv-099.series: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
hv-099.credit: The Howard Mansfield Collection, Purchase, Rogers Fund, 1936

planes.label: Main hall roof and five-storey pagoda
Snowy trees and the Hōzōmon gate
Thunder Gate: pillar and great lantern

rules.title: A frame in front
rules.text: The gate's pillar and its great red lantern, cut off by the edges of the sheet, stand between you and the precinct. The eye looks past them into the snow.

rules.title: Stacked planes
rules.text: Walkers, then trees and the inner gate, then the hall roof and pagoda: each a flat layer, smaller and higher on the sheet as it recedes. There is no single vanishing point.

hv-058.title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
hv-058.series: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
hv-058.credit: The Howard Mansfield Collection, Purchase, Rogers Fund, 1936

rules.title: Bands of space
rules.text: A dark band of cloud printed as a graded wash (bokashi), the far bank as one dark strip, the river as an open field: depth by horizontal bands, like the mist bands (kasumi) of older pictures.

rules.title: The bridge in front
rules.text: The bridge cuts across the near ground on a steep diagonal and runs off both edges of the sheet, so the river opens behind it.

rules.title: A raised far bank
rules.text: The far bank sits high on the sheet, about two-fifths of the way down: you look down on the bridge and across the river, as if from above.

hv-107.title: Fukagawa Susaki and Jūmantsubo
hv-107.series: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
hv-107.credit: The Howard Mansfield Collection, Purchase, Rogers Fund, 1936

rules.title: The eagle in front
rules.text: The eagle fills the top of the sheet and is cut off by its edges. Everything else lies far below it.

rules.title: An eye in the air
rules.text: You look down on the marsh from the eagle's height: plain, fields and water stack up the sheet towards a horizon just below the middle.

rules.title: Bands of ground
rules.text: Snow plain, marsh and water are three horizontal bands, each a flat layer. The graded blue at the bottom (bokashi) closes the nearest band.

ukie.title: Perspective View (uki-e) of a Kabuki Theatre
ukie.credit: Gift of Mrs. Morris Manges, in memory of her husband, Dr. Morris Manges, 1947
ukie.what: Uki-e, 'floating pictures', used the Western rule of one-point perspective: lines running away from you meet at one point on the horizon. Masanobu made this view of a kabuki theatre in 1748. Drawn over the sheet, the floor, walkway and gallery lines gather close to one point on the stage, about two-fifths of the way down; the ceiling beams lean towards points spread along the same horizon. The rule is applied by eye, not exactly. Folded into a box, the sheet holds together from one viewpoint only: swing away and the painted crowd flattens onto the floor. The perspective is a constructed convention, learned from imported pictures.

sources.title: Uki-e (Wikipedia): introduced in the late 1730s; earliest known printed example attributed to Torii Kiyotada, around 1739–40; Masanobu first applied the term
